title: Trade & Protectionism
hook: Should a country trade freely with the world or shield its own industries? This single question has driven economic politics for centuries — and still does.
key_points: Free trade lets goods cross borders with few barriers; protectionism shields domestic industry.
Tariffs (import taxes) and quotas are the main protectionist tools.
Trade can lower prices and boost growth overall, but creates winners and losers within a country.
The politics is fierce because the gains are spread thin while the losses are concentrated.
content_html: Few economic questions are older or more politically charged than how open a country should be to trade. At one pole is free trade: letting goods and services cross borders with few barriers, on the argument that countries prosper by specializing in what they do best and exchanging the rest. At the other is protectionism: using government policy to shield domestic industries from foreign competition. The classic protectionist tools are the tariff — a tax on imported goods that makes them more expensive than local ones — and the quota, a hard limit on how much of something may be imported.
extra_html: Most economists hold that freer trade tends to increase overall prosperity, lowering prices for consumers and raising growth across trading nations. But Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that trade also redistributes: it creates winners and losers within each country. Consumers and competitive export industries gain, while workers and firms in sectors exposed to cheaper imports can lose their livelihoods. This distribution is the key to the politics. The benefits of free trade are real but spread thinly across millions of consumers who barely notice them, while the costs land heavily and visibly on specific communities and industries — so the losers tend to organize and lobby far more intensely than the diffuse winners. That asymmetry, more than pure economics, is why protectionist pressures recur in every era, and why governments perpetually negotiate the balance between openness and protection through trade agreements, tariffs, and disputes.

related.title: Globalization
related.hook: The world's economies have woven together so tightly that a decision in one country ripples through all the others — that deepening interdependence is globalization.

related.title: Global Inequality & Development
related.hook: Where you're born still shapes your life chances more than almost anything else. Closing that gap between rich and poor nations is one of politics' great unfinished projects.

related.title: Markets, Regulation & the Mixed Economy
related.hook: Pure free market or full state control? Almost every country picks neither — they run a mixed economy, and where they draw the line is one of politics' great arguments.

flashcards.back_html: Government policy that shields domestic industries from foreign competition, mainly through tariffs (import taxes) and quotas.

choices.text: A subsidy paid to foreign producers

flashcards.explanation_html: A tariff taxes imports, making foreign goods more expensive and protecting domestic producers from competition.

flashcards.prompt: Why is trade policy so politically contentious?

choices.text: Its overall gains are spread thinly while its losses fall heavily on specific groups
Because no one is ever affected by it
Because trade has no economic effects

flashcards.explanation_html: Diffuse, modest benefits to many consumers are easily outweighed politically by concentrated, intense losses to particular industries.
